knowledge_point.title: Finding a Unit Vector Parallel to a Given Vector in a Diagram

question.:question/problem:
![](/tmp/ca9837-before-after-il1_5v_f/17592186096814/moderate/after-assets/3242c6809f0742449a0a1b2bb8543c93c8cc825bd0eef7e4ac5115407dca8677-prompt.png)

Consider the picture shown above. Find a unit vector that is parallel to $c$. Choose the unit vector in the same direction.
question.:question/worked-solution:
![](/tmp/ca9837-before-after-il1_5v_f/17592186096814/moderate/after-assets/3242c6809f0742449a0a1b2bb8543c93c8cc825bd0eef7e4ac5115407dca8677-solution.png)

In $\bigtriangleup AHB$ we have $\angle AHB=90^\circ$, $AH=3$ and $BH=0.5$. So, the Pythagorean theorem gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
AB &= \sqrt{AH^2+BH^2} \\
&= \sqrt{(3)^2+\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2} \\
&= \sqrt{9+\frac{1}{4}} \\
&= \frac{\sqrt{37}}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the magnitude of $c$ is $\frac{\sqrt{37}}{2}$. Consequently, the unit vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}
u &= \frac{1}{|c|}\cdot c \\
&= \frac{2 \sqrt{37}}{37}c
\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the picture shown above. Find a unit vector that is parallel to $m+n$. Choose the unit vector in the same direction.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we have to find $m+n$. According to the triangle law of addition, the resultant $m+n$ goes from the tail of $m$ to the head of $n$:

![](/tmp/ca9837-before-after-il1_5v_f/17592186096814/hard/after-assets/3521d55887d768e38f81573208b7f00550fd2e19cd049e632dac4d33706401b0-solution.png)

In $\bigtriangleup AHB$ we have $\angle AHB=90^\circ$, $AH=7$ and $BH=2.5$. So, the Pythagorean theorem gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
AB &= \sqrt{AH^2+BH^2} \\
&= \sqrt{(7)^2+\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)^2} \\
&= \sqrt{49+\frac{25}{4}} \\
&= \frac{\sqrt{221}}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the magnitude of $m+n$ is $\frac{\sqrt{221}}{2}$. Consequently, the unit vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}
u &= \frac{1}{|m+n|}\cdot (m+n) \\
&= \frac{2 \sqrt{221}}{221}(m+n)
\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding an Area by Transforming to a Type I Region

question.:question/problem:
Using the change of variables 

$$
u=x - 2 y,\,v=y,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the curve $(x - 2 y)^{2}-(y)=0$ and the line $y=36.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x - 2 y,\,v=y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

Substituting $x - 2 y=u$ and $y=v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
(x - 2 y)^{2}-(y)=0\,⟹\,u^{2}-v=0\,⟹\,v=u^{2}.
$$

while substituting $y=v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
v=36.
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}v &=u^{2} \\ v &=36\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,u=\pm 6\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm 6,36).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,-6\le u\le 6,\,u^{2}\le v\le 36\}.
$$

![](/tmp/ca9837-before-after-il1_5v_f/17592186129197/easy/after-assets/plots/d207c4743dd010bb04819e34.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x}&\frac{∂u}{∂y}\\\frac{∂v}{∂x}&\frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\ &=\begin{vmatrix}1&-2\\0&1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=1\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=(1)^{-1}=1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D dxdy &=\iint_Δ |\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,dudv \\ &=\iint_Δ |1|\,dudv \\ &=1\int_{-6}^{6}[\int_{u^{2}}^{36}dv]du \\ &=1\int_{-6}^{6}[v]_{u^{2}}^{36}du \\ &=1\int_{-6}^{6}(36)-(u^{2})du \\ &=1\int_{-6}^{6}(36 - u^{2})du \\ &=1[- \frac{u^{3}}{3} + 36 u]_{-6}^{6} \\ &=1(((216)+(-72))-((-216)+(72))) \\ &=1(288) \\ &=288\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

question.:question/problem:
Using the change of variables 

$$
u=x - 6 y,\,v=y,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the curve $(x - 6 y)^{2}-(y)=1$ and the line $y=11.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x - 6 y,\,v=y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

Substituting $x - 6 y=u$ and $y=v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
(x - 6 y)^{2}-(y)=1\,⟹\,u^{2}-v=1\,⟹\,v=u^{2} - 1.
$$

while substituting $y=v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
v=11.
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}v &=u^{2} - 1 \\ v &=11\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,u=\pm 2 \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm 2 \sqrt{3},11).$

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,- 2 \sqrt{3}\le u\le 2 \sqrt{3},\,u^{2} - 1\le v\le 11\}.
$$

![](/tmp/ca9837-before-after-il1_5v_f/17592186129197/hard/after-assets/plots/32c61389003668840a6e6151.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x}&\frac{∂u}{∂y}\\\frac{∂v}{∂x}&\frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\ &=\begin{vmatrix}1&-6\\0&1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=1\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=(1)^{-1}=1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D dxdy &=\iint_Δ |\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,dudv \\ &=\iint_Δ |1|\,dudv \\ &=1\int_{- 2 \sqrt{3}}^{2 \sqrt{3}}[\int_{u^{2} - 1}^{11}dv]du \\ &=1\int_{- 2 \sqrt{3}}^{2 \sqrt{3}}[v]_{u^{2} - 1}^{11}du \\ &=1\int_{- 2 \sqrt{3}}^{2 \sqrt{3}}(11)-(u^{2} - 1)du \\ &=1\int_{- 2 \sqrt{3}}^{2 \sqrt{3}}(12 - u^{2})du \\ &=1[- \frac{u^{3}}{3} + 12 u]_{- 2 \sqrt{3}}^{2 \sqrt{3}} \\ &=1(((24 \sqrt{3})+(- 8 \sqrt{3}))-((- 24 \sqrt{3})+(8 \sqrt{3}))) \\ &=1(32 \sqrt{3}) \\ &=32 \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Jacobian of an Inverse Transformation

question.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))$, given that

$$
u=4 x\qquad v=y\qquad w=z.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation

$$
T:(u,v,w)\to(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)),
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T$ is $\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}$.

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}$, the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$.

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}\right)^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=4 & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=0 & \frac{\partial u}{\partial z}=0 \\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial x}=0 & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}=1 & \frac{\partial v}{\partial z}=0 \\ \frac{\partial w}{\partial x}=0 & \frac{\partial w}{\partial y}=0 & \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}&=\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial w}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\end{vmatrix} \\ &=\begin{vmatrix}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=4\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=4\left(1\cdot 1-0\right) \\ &=4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}&=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}\right)^{-1} \\ &=\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Determining the Critical Points of a Transformation

question.:question/problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ \left(w - 3\right)^{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u,\,y(u,v,w)=v,\,z(u,v,w)=\left(w - 3\right)^{2}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =1 & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \frac{∂z}{∂w} & =2 w - 6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 w - 6\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(1)\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 w - 6\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(1)(1\cdot(2 w - 6)-(0)\cdot(0)) \\  & =2 \left(w - 3\right).\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ 2 \left(w - 3\right) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The critical points lie on the plane $w - 3=0.$

The critical points lie on the plane $v - 3=0.$

question.:question/problem:

$$
u=3\left(y-3z\right),\,v=2\left(x+2z\right),\,w=3x-y.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =3\left(1\right) & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =3\left(-3\right) \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =2\left(1\right) & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =2\left(2\right) \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =3 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Scaling the three derivative rows by $3, 2, 1$ multiplies the determinant by $6$.

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 3\left(1\right) & 3\left(-3\right) \\ 2\left(1\right) & 0 & 2\left(2\right) \\ 3 & -1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =6\left(-1\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 0\end{vmatrix}-3\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 3 & -1\end{vmatrix}\right)\\  & =6\left(-1(0-6)-3(-1-0)\right)\\  & =6\left(6+3\right)\\  & =54\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{54}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

$$

$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x,y,z>0.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=3\left(xy\right),\,v(x,y,z)=4\left(yz\right),\,w(x,y,z)=2\left(xz\right).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =3\left(y\right) & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =3\left(x\right) & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =4\left(z\right) & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =4\left(y\right) \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =2\left(z\right) & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =2\left(x\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Scaling the three derivative rows by $3, 4, 2$ multiplies the determinant by $24$.

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}3\left(y\right) & 3\left(x\right) & 0 \\ 0 & 4\left(z\right) & 4\left(y\right) \\ 2\left(z\right) & 0 & 2\left(x\right)\end{vmatrix} \\  & =24\left(y\begin{vmatrix}z & y \\ 0 & x\end{vmatrix}-x\begin{vmatrix}0 & y \\ z & x\end{vmatrix}\right)\\  & =24\left(y(xz-0)-x(0-yz)\right)\\  & =24\left(xyz+xyz\right)\\  & =48 x y z.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}24\left(2xyz\right) & =24\left(2\sqrt{(xyz)^{2}}\right) \\  & =24\left(2\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}}\right) \\  & =24\left(2\sqrt{xy(yz)(xz)}\right) \\  & =24\left(2\sqrt{\left(\frac{u}{3}\right)\left(\frac{v}{4}\right)\left(\frac{w}{2}\right)}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{6}}{24 \sqrt{u v w}}\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:

$$

$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u + 4 v - 3 w,\,y(u,v,w)=2 u^{2} + v,\,z(u,v,w)=u^{2} + 2 u + w.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =1 & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & =4 & \frac{∂x}{∂w} & =-3 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =4 u & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =2 u + 2 & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 4 & -3 \\ 4 u & 1 & 0 \\ 2 u + 2 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(1)\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}+(-4)\begin{vmatrix}4 u & 0 \\ 2 u + 2 & 1\end{vmatrix}+(-3)\begin{vmatrix}4 u & 1 \\ 2 u + 2 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(1)(1\cdot(1)-(0)\cdot(0))+(-4)(4 u\cdot(1)-(0)\cdot(2 u + 2))+(-3)(4 u\cdot(0)-(1)\cdot(2 u + 2)) \\  & =7 - 10 u.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ 7 - 10 u & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The critical points lie on the plane $7 - 10 u=0.$

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}u \\ (v-3){e}^{(w-1)} \\ 2u+(v-3)+3(w-1)\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u,\,y(u,v,w)=(v-3){e}^{(w-1)},\,z(u,v,w)=2u+(v-3)+3(w-1).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & ={e}^{(w-1)} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =(v-3){e}^{(w-1)} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =2 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{(w-1)} & (v-3){e}^{(w-1)} \\ 2 & 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{(w-1)} & (v-3){e}^{(w-1)} \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(3{e}^{(w-1)}-(v-3){e}^{(w-1)}) \\  & ={e}^{(w-1)}(3-(v-3)).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider a small rectangle $Δ$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(4,-3)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta A.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\longrightarrow\begin{bmatrix}\frac{u^{2}}{v}\\u v\end{bmatrix}?
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))\approx\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|\cdot\underbrace{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{\delta A}
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}\end{vmatrix}\\& =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{2 u}{v}&- \frac{u^{2}}{v^{2}}\\v&u\end{vmatrix}\\& =\left(\frac{2 u}{v}\right)\cdot (u)-\left(- \frac{u^{2}}{v^{2}}\right)\cdot (v)\\& =\frac{2u^{2}}{v}+\frac{u^{2}}{v}\\& =\frac{3u^{2}}{v}\\\left.\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|_{(4,-3)} & =\left(\frac{3 u^{2}}{v}\right)\big|_{u=4,v=-3}\\& =\frac{3 (4)^{2}}{(-3)}\\& =-16\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & \approx|-16|\cdot\delta A\\ & =16\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}\end{vmatrix}\\& =\begin{vmatrix}6 \left(2 u + v\right)^{2}&3 \left(2 u + v\right)^{2}\\2 \left(u - 2 v\right)&- 4 \left(u - 2 v\right)\end{vmatrix}\\& =(6 \left(2 u + v\right)^{2})\cdot (- 4 \left(u - 2 v\right))-(3 \left(2 u + v\right)^{2})\cdot (2 \left(u - 2 v\right))\\& =- 120 u^{3} + 120 u^{2} v + 210 u v^{2} + 60 v^{3}\\& =- 30 \left(u - 2 v\right) \left(2 u + v\right)^{2}\\\left.\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|_{(1,-1)} & =\left(- 30 \left(u - 2 v\right) \left(2 u + v\right)^{2}\right)\big|_{u=1,v=-1}\\& =- 30 \left(- 2 (-1) + (1)\right) \left((-1) + 2 (1)\right)^{2}\\& =-90\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & \approx|-90|\cdot\delta A\\ & =90\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

question.:question/problem:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}(u - 1)(v - 2) \\ (u - 1)+(v - 2)\end{bmatrix},

is (locally) orientation-preserving?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that a transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving at the points where the Jacobian determinant is positive:

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}>0.
$$

We have

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}(u - 1)(v - 2) \\ (u - 1)+(v - 2)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}(v - 2) & (u - 1) \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(v - 2)\cdot 1-1\cdot (u - 1) \\  & =(v - 2)-(u - 1).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the required regions, we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}(v - 2)-(u - 1) & >0 \\ (v - 2) & >(u - 1)\end{aligned}

$$
(v - 2)=(u - 1)
$$

defines a line, and the coordinates of, say, $(2,4)$ satisfy the inequality.

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following shows the region in the $uv$-plane where the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}v + \left(u - 1\right)^{2} - 2 \\ - 3 u - \left(v - 2\right)^{2} + 3\end{bmatrix},
$$

is (locally) orientation-reversing?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that a transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing at the points where the Jacobian determinant is negative:

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}<0
$$

We have

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}v + \left(u - 1\right)^{2} - 2 \\ - 3 u - \left(v - 2\right)^{2} + 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} &=\begin{vmatrix}2 u - 2 & 1 \\ -3 & 4 - 2 v\end{vmatrix} \\ &=(2 u - 2)\cdot (4 - 2 v)-(1)\cdot (-3) \\ &=- 4 u v + 8 u + 4 v - 5.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the required regions, we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}- 4 u v + 8 u + 4 v - 5 &<0 \\ \left(u - 1\right) \left(v - 2\right) > \frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the solution $v > 2 + \frac{3}{4 \left(u - 1\right)}$ for $u>1$ and $v < 2 + \frac{3}{4 \left(u - 1\right)}$ for $u<1.$ At $u=1,$ the Jacobian is positive, so this line is excluded from the required region.

Notice that the equation

$$
v = 2 + \frac{3}{4 \left(u - 1\right)}
$$

defines a hyperbola.

Therefore, the region where the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing must be the following:

knowledge_point.title: Evaluating a Line Integral Using Stokes' Theorem

question.:question/problem: Let $C$ be the intersection of the cylinder $x^2+y^2=9$ and the plane $z=1$. The curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above. Given that $\text{curl}\,F=\langle - 4 x z,\,- 4 y z,\,4 x + 4 z^{2}\rangle$, use Stokes' theorem to evaluate $\oint_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C.$ One such surface is our graph $S$ with the equation

$$
z=g(x,y)=1.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial g}{\partial x}&=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(1\right)=0\\
\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(1\right)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F|_{z=g(x,y)}&=\langle - 4 x z,\,- 4 y z,\,4 x + 4 z^{2}\rangle|_{z=1}\\
&=\langle - 4 x,\,- 4 y,\,4 x + 4\rangle\\
&=\langle - 4 x,\,- 4 y,\,4 x + 4\rangle.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_S\text{curl}\,F\cdot\mathrm{d}S&=\iint_D(-P g_x-Q g_y+R)\,\mathrm{d}A\\
&=\iint_D\left(-\left(- 4 x\right)\left(0\right)-\left(- 4 y\right)\left(0\right)+\left(4 x + 4\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}A\\
&=\iint_D\left((0)+(0)+(4 x + 4)\right)\,\mathrm{d}A\\
&=\iint_D\left(4 x + 4\right)\,\mathrm{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is the region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.
Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle $x^2+y^2=9.$ Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x=r\cos\theta,\quad y=r\sin\theta,\quad \mathrm{d}A=r\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta,
$$

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D\left(4 x + 4\right)\,\mathrm{d}A
&=\int_0^{3}\int_0^{2\pi}\left(4 r \cos{\left(\theta \right)} + 4\right)r\,\mathrm{d}\theta\,\mathrm{d}r\\
&=\int_0^{3}\int_0^{2\pi}\left(4 r^{2} \cos{\left(\theta \right)} + 4 r\right)\,\mathrm{d}\theta\,\mathrm{d}r\\
&=\int_0^{3}\left[4 r^{2} \sin{\left(\theta \right)} + 4 r \theta\right]_0^{2\pi}\,\mathrm{d}r\\
&=\int_0^{3}\left[\left(8 \pi r\right)-\left(0\right)\right]\,\mathrm{d}r\\
&=\int_0^{3}\left(8 \pi r\right)\,\mathrm{d}r\\
&=\left[4 \pi r^{2}\right]_0^{3}\\
&=\left[\left(36 \pi\right)\right]-\left[\left(0\right)\right]\\
&=36 \pi.\end{aligned}
$$

&=\langle - 4 y,\,8 x - 4 y + 4,\,- 8 x\rangle.\end{aligned}$$

So, we have

$$\begin{aligned}\iint_S\text{curl}\,F\cdot\mathrm{d}S&=\iint_D(-P g_x-Q g_y+R)\,\mathrm{d}A\\
&=\iint_D\left(-\left(- 4 y\right)\left(2\right)-\left(8 x - 4 y + 4\right)\left(-1\right)+\left(- 8 x\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}A\\
&=\iint_D\left((8 y)+(8 x - 4 y + 4)+(- 8 x)\right)\,\mathrm{d}A\\
&=\iint_D\left(4 y + 4\right)\,\mathrm{d}A.\end{aligned}$$

where $D$ is the region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.
Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle $x^2+y^2=9.$ Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$x=r\cos\theta,\quad y=r\sin\theta,\quad \mathrm{d}A=r\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta,$$

we obtain

$$\begin{aligned}\iint_D\left(4 y + 4\right)\,\mathrm{d}A
&=\int_0^{3}\int_0^{2\pi}\left(4 r \sin{\left(\theta \right)} + 4\right)r\,\mathrm{d}\theta\,\mathrm{d}r\\
&=\int_0^{3}\int_0^{2\pi}\left(4 r^{2} \sin{\left(\theta \right)} + 4 r\right)\,\mathrm{d}\theta\,\mathrm{d}r\\
&=\int_0^{3}\left[- 4 r^{2} \cos{\left(\theta \right)} + 4 r \theta\right]_0^{2\pi}\,\mathrm{d}r\\
&=\int_0^{3}\left[\left(- 4 r^{2} + 8 \pi r\right)-\left(- 4 r^{2}\right)\right]\,\mathrm{d}r\\
&=\int_0^{3}\left(8 \pi r\right)\,\mathrm{d}r\\
&=\left[4 \pi r^{2}\right]_0^{3}\\
&=\left[\left(36 \pi\right)\right]-\left[\left(0\right)\right]\\
&=36 \pi.\end{aligned}$$

knowledge_point.title: Evaluating a Line Integral Using Stokes' Theorem

question.:question/problem: Let $C$ be the intersection of the surface $z=\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$ and the vertical column over $D$, where $-3\leq x\leq 0$ and $0\leq y\leq x + 3$. The curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above. Given that $\text{curl}\,F=\langle 0,\,- 4 z^{3},\,0\rangle$, use Stokes' theorem to write down the integral that gives the circulation along $C.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C.$ One such surface is our graph $S$ with the equation

$$
z=g(x,y)=\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial g}{\partial x}&=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}\right)=\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}\\
\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}\right)=\frac{y}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F|_{z=g(x,y)}&=\langle 0,\,- 4 z^{3},\,0\rangle|_{z=\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}\\
&=\langle 0,\,- 4 \left(x^{2} + y^{2}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}},\,0\rangle\\
&=\langle 0,\,- 4 x^{2} \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}} - 4 y^{2} \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}},\,0\rangle.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_S\text{curl}\,F\cdot\mathrm{d}S&=\iint_D(-P g_x-Q g_y+R)\,\mathrm{d}A\\
&=\iint_D\left(-\left(0\right)\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}\right)-\left(- 4 x^{2} \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}} - 4 y^{2} \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}\right)\left(\frac{y}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}\right)+\left(0\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}A\\
&=\iint_D\left((0)+\left(\frac{y \left(4 x^{2} \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}} + 4 y^{2} \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}\right)}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}\right)+(0)\right)\,\mathrm{d}A\\
&=\iint_D\left(4 y \left(x^{2} + y^{2}\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is the region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

![](/tmp/ca9837-before-after-il1_5v_f/17592186133927/moderate/after-assets/region-bef98e33c36833facd.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\int_{-3}^{0}\int_{0}^{x + 3}\left(4 y \left(x^{2} + y^{2}\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Sketching a Two-Dimensional Vector Field

question.:question/problem:
Which diagram represents

$$
\mathbf F(x,y)=\left(x^{2}\right)\,i+\left(2y\right)\,j
$$

at $A=(-2,2)$, $B=(2,1)$, $C=(0,3)$? All diagrams use one unit per grid interval.

Evaluate both components at each point, then place the tail of its vector at that point.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write $\mathbf F=P\,i+Q\,j$. Substitute into each component, then combine the results:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(-2,2)&=(1)(-2)^{2}=4 \\
Q(-2,2)&=(2)(2)=4 \\
\mathbf F(-2,2)&=4\,i+4\,j \\
P(2,1)&=(1)(2)^{2}=4 \\
Q(2,1)&=(2)(1)=2 \\
\mathbf F(2,1)&=4\,i+2\,j \\
P(0,3)&=(1)(0)^{2}=0 \\
Q(0,3)&=(2)(3)=6 \\
\mathbf F(0,3)&=6\,j
\end{aligned}
$$

The first component gives the horizontal displacement and the second gives the vertical displacement. Place each tail at its labeled point. A zero component gives no displacement along that axis; a zero vector stays at its tail.

knowledge_point.title: Constructing Surface Integrals Over Parametric Surfaces

question.:question/problem:
$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

Consider the surface integral of the function 
$f(x,y,z)=- x^{2} + 3 y z$ 
over the parametric surface 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨2 u,\,u + v,\,v^{2}⟩
$$

for $(u,v)\in D⊆{R}^{2}.$ What is the missing expression? Choose an integrand equal to the required expression as a function on $D$.

*Hint: You can use the fact that $‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=\sqrt{20 v^{2} + 4}.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=\sqrt{20 v^{2} + 4}.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(- x^{2} + 3 y z)\,{|}_{x=2 u\,y=u + v\,z=v^{2}} \\  & =-(2 u\cdot 2 u)+3\cdot (u+v)\cdot v^{2} \\  & =- 4 u^{2} + 3 v^{2} \left(u + v\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\left(- 4 u^{2} + 3 v^{2} \left(u + v\right)\right) \sqrt{20 v^{2} + 4}\,\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the surface integral of the function 
$f(x,y,z)=x - 3 y^{2} z$ 
over the parametric surface 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨2 u v,\,- 3 u,\,3 u - 3 v^{2}⟩
$$

for $(u,v)\in D⊆{R}^{2}.$ What is the missing expression? Choose an integrand equal to the required expression as a function on $D$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(2 u v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(- 3 u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(3 u - 3 v^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2 v,\,-3,\,3⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(2 u v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(- 3 u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(3 u - 3 v^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2 u,\,0,\,- 6 v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 2 v & -3 & 3 \\ 2 u & 0 & - 6 v\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 3 \\ 0 & - 6 v\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}2 v & 3 \\ 2 u & - 6 v\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}2 v & -3 \\ 2 u & 0\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨18 v,\,6 u + 12 v^{2},\,6 u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨18 v,\,6 u + 12 v^{2},\,6 u⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(18 v)^{2}+(6 u + 12 v^{2})^{2}+(6 u)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{72 u^{2} + 144 u v^{2} + 144 v^{4} + 324 v^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(x - 3 y^{2} z)\,{|}_{x=2 u v\,y=- 3 u\,z=3 u - 3 v^{2}} \\  & =2 u v-3\cdot (- 3 u)^{2}\cdot (3 u - 3 v^{2}) \\  & =- 81 u^{3} + 81 u^{2} v^{2} + 2 u v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\left(- 81 u^{3} + 81 u^{2} v^{2} + 2 u v\right) \sqrt{72 u^{2} + 144 u v^{2} + 144 v^{4} + 324 v^{2}}\,\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Sketching a Two-Dimensional Vector Field

question.:question/problem:
Which diagram represents

$$
\mathbf F(x,y)=\left(-y-x\right)\,i+\left(x-y\right)\,j
$$

at $A=(2,1)$, $B=(0,-1)$, $C=(-1,0)$? All diagrams use one unit per grid interval.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write $\mathbf F=P\,i+Q\,j$. Substitute into each component, then combine the results:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(2,1)&=(-1)(1)-(1)(2)=-3 \\
Q(2,1)&=(1)(2)+(-1)(1)=1 \\
\mathbf F(2,1)&=-3\,i+j \\
P(0,-1)&=(-1)(-1)-(1)(0)=1 \\
Q(0,-1)&=(1)(0)+(-1)(-1)=1 \\
\mathbf F(0,-1)&=i+j \\
P(-1,0)&=(-1)(0)-(1)(-1)=1 \\
Q(-1,0)&=(1)(-1)+(-1)(0)=-1 \\
\mathbf F(-1,0)&=i-j
\end{aligned}
$$

The first component gives the horizontal displacement and the second gives the vertical displacement. Place each tail at its labeled point. A zero component gives no displacement along that axis; a zero vector stays at its tail.

knowledge_point.title: Constructing Surface Integrals Over Parametric Surfaces

question.:question/problem:
$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

Consider the surface integral of the function 
$f(x,y,z)=x - 3 y^{2} z$ 
over the parametric surface 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨2 u v,\,- u,\,- v^{2}⟩
$$

for $(u,v)\in D⊆{R}^{2}.$ What is the missing expression? Choose an integrand equal to the required expression as a function on $D$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(2 u v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(- u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(- v^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2 v,\,-1,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(2 u v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(- u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(- v^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2 u,\,0,\,- 2 v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 2 v & -1 & 0 \\ 2 u & 0 & - 2 v\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & - 2 v\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}2 v & 0 \\ 2 u & - 2 v\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}2 v & -1 \\ 2 u & 0\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨2 v,\,4 v^{2},\,2 u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨2 v,\,4 v^{2},\,2 u⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(2 v)^{2}+(4 v^{2})^{2}+(2 u)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4 u^{2} + 16 v^{4} + 4 v^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(x - 3 y^{2} z)\,{|}_{x=2 u v\,y=- u\,z=- v^{2}} \\  & =(2 u v)-3\cdot (-u)^{2}\cdot (-v^{2}) \\  & =3 u^{2} v^{2} + 2 u v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\left(3 u^{2} v^{2} + 2 u v\right) \sqrt{4 u^{2} + 16 v^{4} + 4 v^{2}}\,\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

:answer-field/choices.:answer/value: \left(3 u^{2} v^{2} + 2 u v\right) \left(4 u^{2} + 16 v^{4} + 4 v^{2}\right)

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral

$$
\iint_S(x-y)\,\text{d}S,
$$

where $r(u,v)=⟨2u+2v,\,2u-2v,\,3v⟩$ for $0\le u\le 3$ and $0\le v\le 3.$

*Hint: $‖r_u′\times r_v′‖=2\sqrt{34}.$*

{{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product is

$$
‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=2\sqrt{34}.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
f(r(u,v))=(2u+2v)-(2u-2v)=4v.
$$

Therefore, our surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_S(x-y)\,\text{d}S&=\iint_D f(r(u,v))‖r_u′\times r_v′‖\,\text{d}A\\&=2\sqrt{34}\iint_D 4v\,\text{d}A\\&=2\sqrt{34}\int_0^{3}4v\,\text{d}v\cdot\int_0^{3}1\,\text{d}u\\&=2\sqrt{34}[2v^{2}]_0^{3}[u]_0^{3}\\&=2\sqrt{34}(18-0)(3-0)\\&=108\sqrt{34}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}2xz\,\text{d}S,
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
x=u,\,y=u+v,\,z=2v
$$

for $0\le u\le 3$ and $0\le v\le \frac{5}{2}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,u+v,\,2v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,-2,\,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨2,\,-2,\,1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+4+1} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =2xz\,{|}_{x=u\,y=u+v\,z=2v} \\  & =2u(2v) \\  & =4uv\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 3,\,0\le v\le \frac{5}{2}\},
$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}2xz\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,4uv\cdot 3\,\text{d}A \\  & =3{∬}_{D}\,4uv\,\text{d}A \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{3}2u\,\text{d}u\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\frac{5}{2}}2v\,\text{d}v \\  & =3\cdot [{u}^{2}]_{0}^{3}\cdot [{v}^{2}]_{0}^{\frac{5}{2}} \\  & =3[(9)-(0)]\cdot [\left(\frac{25}{4}\right)-(0)] \\  & =3\cdot 9\cdot \frac{25}{4} \\  & =\frac{675}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product is

$$
‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=2\sqrt{2}.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(3x-2y+3z)\,{|}_{x=2u+v\,y=2u+v\,z=-v} \\  & =3(2u+v)-2(2u+v)+3(-v) \\  & =2(u-v)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,2(u-v)\cdot 2\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,(u-v)\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{\frac{5}{2}}^{3}({\int }_{-\frac{3}{2}}^{\frac{3}{2}}u-v\,\text{d}u)\text{d}v \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{\frac{5}{2}}^{3}{[\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}-vu]}_{-\frac{3}{2}}^{\frac{3}{2}}\text{d}v \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{\frac{5}{2}}^{3}[((-\frac{3v}{2})+\frac{9}{8})-(\frac{3v}{2}+\frac{9}{8})]\text{d}v \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{\frac{5}{2}}^{3}(0-3v)\text{d}v \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{[-\frac{3{v}^{2}}{2}]}_{\frac{5}{2}}^{3} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}[((-\frac{27}{2}))-((-\frac{75}{8}))] \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\cdot (-\frac{33}{8}) \\  & =-\frac{33\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The field must be perpendicular to every regular level curve. One compatible function, used here to check the geometric match, is $f(x,y)=y^2+\left(x+1\right)$.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)&=c\\y^2+\left(x+1\right)&=c\\x&=-1+c-y^2\end{aligned}
$$

These level curves are left-opening parabolas. With $y$ fixed, moving right increases the function. With $x$ fixed, moving away from $y=0$ increases it. Unlabeled contours do not specify which side has larger values; the required test for these choices is perpendicularity, including at off-axis points.

A derivative check gives $\nabla f=\left\langle 1,2y\right\rangle$. These directions are normal to the level curves and point toward increasing values. Other curve shapes have a different normal direction somewhere; a reversed field, if offered, points downhill.

question.:question/problem:
Consider the region $D$ in the $xy$-plane, given by

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,3\le 2x+5y\le 8,\,7\le x+3y\le 8\}.
$$

By performing the change of variables $u=2x+5y$ and $v=x+3y,$ the integral

$$
{∬}_{D}{e}^{x+y}\,dx\,dy
$$

can be written in terms of $u$ and $v$ as
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy={∬}_{Δ}f(x(u,v),y(u,v))|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|du\,dv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=2x+5y,\,v=x+3y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,3\le u\le 8,\,7\le v\le 8\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 5 \\ 1 & \text{ }\text{ }3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

In this case, we first need to solve the transformation equations

$$
u=2x+5y,\,v=x+3y
$$

 
for $x$ and $y$, which gives

$$
x=3u-5v,\,y=2v-u.
$$

 

Now, performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{e}^{x+y}\,dx\,dy & ={∬}_{Δ}{e}^{3u-5v+2v-u}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{e}^{2u-3v}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{e}^{2u-3v}\cdot |1|\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{7}^{8}{\int }_{3}^{8}{e}^{2u-3v}\,du\,dv.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Using the change of variables $u=\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}$ and $v=xy,$ evaluate the double integral

$$
{∬}_{D}(xy)^{2}\,dx\,dy,
$$

where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}\le y\le 9{x}^{2},\,5\le xy\le 6\}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|du\,dv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=\frac{y}{{x}^{2}},\,v=xy
$$

 
gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 9,\,5\le v\le 6\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-\frac{2y}{{x}^{3}} & \frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ y & \text{ }\text{ }x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{3y}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{\left(-\frac{3y}{{x}^{2}}\right)}=-\frac{1}{3u}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(xy)^{2}\,dx\,dy & ={∬}_{Δ}{v}^{2}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{v}^{2}\cdot |\frac{1}{3u}|\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{5}^{6}{\int }_{1}^{9}\frac{{v}^{2}}{u}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{5}^{6}{v}^{2}[{\int }_{1}^{9}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u]\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{5}^{6}{v}^{2}[\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|\,{|}_{1}^{9}]dv \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{5}^{6}{v}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡9-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\,dv \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{3}{\int }_{5}^{6}{v}^{2}\,dv \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{3}{v}^{3}\,{|}_{5}^{6} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{9}\cdot (216-125) \\  & =\frac{182\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Using the change of variables $u=\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}$ and $v=xy,$ evaluate the double integral

$$
{∬}_{D}xy\,dx\,dy,
$$

where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}\le y\le 9{x}^{2},\,7\le xy\le 8\}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|du\,dv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=\frac{y}{{x}^{2}},\,v=xy
$$

 
gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 9,\,7\le v\le 8\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-\frac{2y}{{x}^{3}} & \frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ y & \text{ }\text{ }x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{3y}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{\left(-\frac{3y}{{x}^{2}}\right)}=-\frac{1}{3u}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}xy\,dx\,dy & ={∬}_{Δ}v|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}v\cdot |\frac{1}{3u}|\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{7}^{8}{\int }_{1}^{9}\frac{v}{u}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{7}^{8}v[{\int }_{1}^{9}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u]\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{7}^{8}v[\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|\,{|}_{1}^{9}]dv \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{7}^{8}v(\operatorname{ln}⁡9-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\,dv \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{3}{\int }_{7}^{8}v\,dv \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}\,{|}_{7}^{8} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{3}\cdot (64-49) \\  & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡3.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral

$$
\iint_D x + y\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y
$$

where $D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le 5,\quad 0\le x + y\le 6\}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$
0\le x\le 5,\quad 0\le x + y\le 6,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables

$$
u=x\,\text{and}\,v=x + y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v):0\le u\le 5,\,0\le v\le 6\}.
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\\\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}&\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\end{vmatrix}\\&=\left|\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0\\1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\right|\\&=1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}\right)^{-1}=1=1.
$$

Note that $\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\ne0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

Solving the transformation equations gives $x=u,\ y=- u + v$, so the transformation is one-to-one on this domain.

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D x + y\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y & =\iint_\Delta v\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}v \\ & =\iint_\Delta \left(v\right)\cdot \left(1\right)\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}v \\ & =1\int_{0}^{6} [\int_{0}^{5} v\,\mathrm{d}u]\,\mathrm{d}v \\ & =1\int_{0}^{6} v[\int_{0}^{5} 1\,\mathrm{d}u]\,\mathrm{d}v \\ & =1\int_{0}^{6} v\left[u\right]_{0}^{5}\,\mathrm{d}v \\ & =1\int_{0}^{6} v\left(\left(5\right)-(\left(0\right))\right)\,\mathrm{d}v \\ & =\left(1\right)\cdot \left(5\right)\int_{0}^{6} v\,\mathrm{d}v \\ & =\left(1\right)\cdot \left(5\right)\left[\frac{v^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{6} \\ & =\left(1\right)\cdot \left(5\right)\left(\left(18\right)-(\left(0\right))\right) \\ & =\left(1\right)\cdot \left(5\right)\cdot \left(18\right) \\ & =90\end{aligned}
$$

$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$

$$

suggest that we use the change of variables

$$
u=\frac{x}{\sqrt{25 - y^{2}}}\,\text{and}\,v=y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v):2\le u\le 3,\,2\le v\le 3\}.
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\\\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}&\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\end{vmatrix}\\&=\left|\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{25 - y^{2}}} & \frac{x y}{\left(25 - y^{2}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}\\0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\right|\\&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{25 - y^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}\right)^{-1}=\sqrt{25 - y^{2}}=\sqrt{25 - v^{2}}.
$$

Note that $\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\ne0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

$$

where $D=\{(x,y):0\le \frac{x}{\sqrt{9 - y^{2}}}\le 3,\quad -2\le y\le 2\}.$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$
0\le \frac{x}{\sqrt{9 - y^{2}}}\le 3,\quad -2\le y\le 2,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables

$$
u=\frac{x}{\sqrt{9 - y^{2}}}\,\text{and}\,v=y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v):0\le u\le 3,\,-2\le v\le 2\}.
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\\\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}&\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\end{vmatrix}\\&=\left|\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{9 - y^{2}}} & \frac{x y}{\left(9 - y^{2}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}\\0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\right|\\&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{9 - y^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}\right)^{-1}=\sqrt{9 - y^{2}}=\sqrt{9 - v^{2}}.
$$

Note that $\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\ne0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D x y^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y & =\iint_\Delta u v^{2} \sqrt{9 - v^{2}}\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}v \\ & =\iint_\Delta \left(u v^{2} \sqrt{9 - v^{2}}\right)\cdot \left(\sqrt{9 - v^{2}}\right)\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}v \\ & =\iint_\Delta u v^2(9-v^2)\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}v \\ & =\int_{0}^{3} \left(u\right)[\int_{-2}^{2} - v^{4} + 9 v^{2}\,\mathrm{d}v]\,\mathrm{d}u \\ & =1\int_{0}^{3} \left(u\right)\left[- \frac{v^{5}}{5} + 3 v^{3}\right]_{-2}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}u \\ & =1\int_{0}^{3} \left(u\right)\left(\left(24\right)+\left(- \frac{32}{5}\right)-(\left(-24\right)+\left(\frac{32}{5}\right))\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\ & =\left(1\right)\cdot \left(\frac{176}{5}\right)\int_{0}^{3} u\,\mathrm{d}u \\ & =\left(1\right)\cdot \left(\frac{176}{5}\right)\left[\frac{u^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{3} \\ & =\left(1\right)\cdot \left(\frac{176}{5}\right)\left(\left(\frac{9}{2}\right)-(\left(0\right))\right) \\ & =\left(1\right)\cdot \left(\frac{9}{2}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{176}{5}\right) \\ & =\frac{792}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Evaluating a Triple Integral Using a Change of Variables

question.:question/problem:
Use the change of variables 

$$
u=2 x + y,\quad v=y - 2 z,\quad w=4 z
$$

to evaluate the triple integral

$$
\iiint_R \left(\left(2 x + y\right) \left(y - 2 z\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}V,
$$

 
where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z):0\le 2 x + y\le 3,\quad 0\le y - 2 z\le 3,\quad 0\le z\le 2\}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=2 x + y,\quad v=y - 2 z,\quad w=4 z
$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v,w):0\le u\le 3,\quad 0\le v\le 3,\quad 0\le w\le 8\}.
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial w}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left(4\right)(-1)^{3+3}\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left(4\right)\left(\left(2\right)\cdot \left(1\right)-\left(1\right)\cdot \left(0\right)\right) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}\right)^{-1}=\frac{1}{8}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iiint_R \left(\left(2 x + y\right) \left(y - 2 z\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}V & =\iiint_\Delta \left(u v\right)\cdot \left|\frac{1}{8}\right|\,\mathrm{d}u\mathrm{d}v\mathrm{d}w \\  & =\iiint_\Delta \left(\frac{u v}{8}\right)\,\mathrm{d}u\mathrm{d}v\mathrm{d}w \\  & =\int_{0}^{3}\int_{0}^{3}\int_{0}^{8}\left(\frac{u v}{8}\right)\,\mathrm{d}w\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{3}\int_{0}^{3}\left(\left[\frac{u v w}{8}\right]_{w=0}^{w=8}\right)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{3}\int_{0}^{3}\left(\left(\frac{u v \left(8\right)}{8}\right)-\left(\frac{u v \left(0\right)}{8}\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{3}\int_{0}^{3}\left(\left(u v\right)-\left(0\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{3}\int_{0}^{3}\left(u v\right)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{3}\left(\left[\frac{u v^{2}}{2}\right]_{v=0}^{v=3}\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{3}\left(\left(\frac{u \left(3\right)^{2}}{2}\right)-\left(\frac{u \left(0\right)^{2}}{2}\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{3}\left(\left(\frac{9 u}{2}\right)-\left(0\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{3}\left(\frac{9 u}{2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\left[\frac{9 u^{2}}{4}\right]_{u=0}^{u=3} \\  & =\left(\frac{9 \left(3\right)^{2}}{4}\right)-\left(\frac{9 \left(0\right)^{2}}{4}\right) \\  & =\left(\frac{81}{4}\right)-\left(0\right) \\  & =\frac{81}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$
\iint_D 2 y^{2} \left(3 x + y\right)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y,
$$

where $D$ is the quadrilateral region with vertices $(0,1)$, $(1,1)$, $(\frac{1}{3},3)$ and $(- \frac{2}{3},3)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)=2 y^{2} \left(3 x + y\right)
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=3 x + y,\qquad v=y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
T^{-1}:(x,y)\mapsto (u(x,y),v(x,y)).
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T^{-1}(0,1)&=(\left(3\right)\cdot \left(0\right)+\left(1\right)\cdot \left(1\right)+\left(0\right),\left(0\right)\cdot \left(0\right)+\left(1\right)\cdot \left(1\right)+\left(0\right)) \\ &=(1,1) \\ T^{-1}(1,1)&=(\left(3\right)\cdot \left(1\right)+\left(1\right)\cdot \left(1\right)+\left(0\right),\left(0\right)\cdot \left(1\right)+\left(1\right)\cdot \left(1\right)+\left(0\right)) \\ &=(4,1) \\ T^{-1}(\frac{1}{3},3)&=(\left(3\right)\cdot \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)+\left(1\right)\cdot \left(3\right)+\left(0\right),\left(0\right)\cdot \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)+\left(1\right)\cdot \left(3\right)+\left(0\right)) \\ &=(4,3) \\ T^{-1}(- \frac{2}{3},3)&=(\left(3\right)\cdot \left(- \frac{2}{3}\right)+\left(1\right)\cdot \left(3\right)+\left(0\right),\left(0\right)\cdot \left(- \frac{2}{3}\right)+\left(1\right)\cdot \left(3\right)+\left(0\right)) \\ &=(1,3)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v):1\le u\le 4,\ 1\le v\le 3\}
$$

![](/tmp/ca9837-before-after-il1_5v_f/17592186198374/easy/after-assets/6f84f3326e21ac887e1e.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}&=\begin{vmatrix}\partial u/\partial x&\partial u/\partial y\\\partial v/\partial x&\partial v/\partial y\end{vmatrix} \\ &=\begin{vmatrix}3&1\\0&1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=3.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}\right)^{-1}=\frac{1}{3}
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

Solving these affine equations also gives

$$
x=\frac{u}{3} - \frac{v}{3},\qquad y=v.
$$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D 2 y^{2} \left(3 x + y\right)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y&=\iint_\Delta 2 u v^{2}\,\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}v \\ &=\iint_\Delta 2 u v^{2}\,\left|\frac{1}{3}\right|\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}v \\ &=\frac{2}{3}\cdot \int_{1}^{3}\int_{1}^{4}u v^{2}\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}v \\ &=\frac{2}{3}\cdot \int_{1}^{3}v^{2}\,\mathrm{d}v\cdot \int_{1}^{4}u\,\mathrm{d}u \\ &=\frac{2}{3}\cdot \left[\frac{v^{3}}{3}\right]_{1}^{3}\cdot \left[\frac{u^{2}}{2}\right]_{1}^{4} \\ &=\frac{2}{3}\cdot \left(\left(3\right)^{3}/3-\left(\left(1\right)^{3}/3\right)\right)\cdot \left(\left(4\right)^{2}/2-\left(\left(1\right)^{2}/2\right)\right) \\ &=\frac{2}{3}\cdot \left(\left(9\right)-\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\right)\cdot \left(\left(8\right)-\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\right) \\ &=\frac{2}{3}\cdot \left(\frac{26}{3}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{15}{2}\right) \\ &=\frac{130}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv

$$

$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

$$

$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=x - \frac{y}{4},\quad v=\frac{y}{4},\quad w=\frac{z}{4}
$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\iiint_R \left(x - \frac{y}{4} + \frac{z}{4}\right)\,\mathrm{d}V & =\iiint_\Delta \left(u + w\right)\cdot \left|16\right|\,\mathrm{d}u\mathrm{d}v\mathrm{d}w \\  & =\iiint_\Delta \left(16 u + 16 w\right)\,\mathrm{d}u\mathrm{d}v\mathrm{d}w \\  & =\int_{1}^{3}\int_{1}^{3}\int_{\frac{1}{4}}^{\frac{3}{4}}\left(16 u + 16 w\right)\,\mathrm{d}w\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{1}^{3}\int_{1}^{3}\left(\left[16 u w + 8 w^{2}\right]_{w=\frac{1}{4}}^{w=\frac{3}{4}}\right)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{1}^{3}\int_{1}^{3}\left(\left(8 \left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^{2}\right)-\left(8 \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{2}\right)+\left(16 u \left(\frac{3}{4}\right)\right)-\left(16 u \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{1}^{3}\int_{1}^{3}\left(\left(\frac{9}{2}\right)-\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+\left(12 u\right)-\left(4 u\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{1}^{3}\int_{1}^{3}\left(8 u + 4\right)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{1}^{3}\left(\left[v \left(8 u + 4\right)\right]_{v=1}^{v=3}\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{1}^{3}\left(\left(4 \left(3\right)\right)-\left(4 \left(1\right)\right)+\left(8 u \left(3\right)\right)-\left(8 u \left(1\right)\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{1}^{3}\left(\left(12\right)-\left(4\right)+\left(24 u\right)-\left(8 u\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{1}^{3}\left(16 u + 8\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\left[8 u^{2} + 8 u\right]_{u=1}^{u=3} \\  & =\left(8 \left(3\right)\right)-\left(8 \left(1\right)\right)+\left(8 \left(3\right)^{2}\right)-\left(8 \left(1\right)^{2}\right) \\  & =\left(24\right)-\left(8\right)+\left(72\right)-\left(8\right) \\  & =80\end{aligned}
$$

$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}\right)^{-1}=16.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\iiint_R \left(x - \frac{y}{4} + \frac{z}{4}\right)\,\mathrm{d}V & =\iiint_\Delta \left(u + w\right)\cdot \left|16\right|\,\mathrm{d}u\mathrm{d}v\mathrm{d}w \\  & =\iiint_\Delta \left(16 u + 16 w\right)\,\mathrm{d}u\mathrm{d}v\mathrm{d}w \\  & =\int_{0}^{3}\int_{0}^{3}\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(16 u + 16 w\right)\,\mathrm{d}w\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{3}\int_{0}^{3}\left(\left[16 u w + 8 w^{2}\right]_{w=0}^{w=\frac{1}{2}}\right)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{3}\int_{0}^{3}\left(\left(8 \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}\right)-\left(8 \left(0\right)^{2}\right)+\left(16 u \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\right)-\left(16 u \left(0\right)\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{3}\int_{0}^{3}\left(\left(2\right)-\left(0\right)+\left(8 u\right)-\left(0\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{3}\int_{0}^{3}\left(8 u + 2\right)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{3}\left(\left[v \left(8 u + 2\right)\right]_{v=0}^{v=3}\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{3}\left(\left(2 \left(3\right)\right)-\left(2 \left(0\right)\right)+\left(8 u \left(3\right)\right)-\left(8 u \left(0\right)\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{3}\left(\left(6\right)-\left(0\right)+\left(24 u\right)-\left(0\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{3}\left(24 u + 6\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\left[12 u^{2} + 6 u\right]_{u=0}^{u=3} \\  & =\left(6 \left(3\right)\right)-\left(6 \left(0\right)\right)+\left(12 \left(3\right)^{2}\right)-\left(12 \left(0\right)^{2}\right) \\  & =\left(18\right)-\left(0\right)+\left(108\right)-\left(0\right) \\  & =126\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$
\iint_D 2 \left(x + y\right) e^{x + 4 y}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y,
$$

where $D$ is the quadrilateral region with vertices $(\frac{4}{3},- \frac{1}{3})$, $(\frac{16}{3},- \frac{4}{3})$, $(\frac{13}{3},- \frac{1}{3})$ and $(\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3})$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)=2 \left(x + y\right) e^{x + 4 y}
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=x + y,\qquad v=x + 4 y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
T^{-1}:(x,y)\mapsto (u(x,y),v(x,y)).
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T^{-1}(\frac{4}{3},- \frac{1}{3})&=(\left(1\right)\cdot \left(\frac{4}{3}\right)+\left(1\right)\cdot \left(- \frac{1}{3}\right)+\left(0\right),\left(1\right)\cdot \left(\frac{4}{3}\right)+\left(4\right)\cdot \left(- \frac{1}{3}\right)+\left(0\right)) \\ &=(1,0) \\ T^{-1}(\frac{16}{3},- \frac{4}{3})&=(\left(1\right)\cdot \left(\frac{16}{3}\right)+\left(1\right)\cdot \left(- \frac{4}{3}\right)+\left(0\right),\left(1\right)\cdot \left(\frac{16}{3}\right)+\left(4\right)\cdot \left(- \frac{4}{3}\right)+\left(0\right)) \\ &=(4,0) \\ T^{-1}(\frac{13}{3},- \frac{1}{3})&=(\left(1\right)\cdot \left(\frac{13}{3}\right)+\left(1\right)\cdot \left(- \frac{1}{3}\right)+\left(0\right),\left(1\right)\cdot \left(\frac{13}{3}\right)+\left(4\right)\cdot \left(- \frac{1}{3}\right)+\left(0\right)) \\ &=(4,3) \\ T^{-1}(\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3})&=(\left(1\right)\cdot \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)+\left(1\right)\cdot \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)+\left(0\right),\left(1\right)\cdot \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)+\left(4\right)\cdot \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)+\left(0\right)) \\ &=(1,3)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v):1\le u\le 4,\ 0\le v\le 3\}
$$

![](/tmp/ca9837-before-after-il1_5v_f/17592186198374/hard/after-assets/9fba0afa076020d33258.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}&=\begin{vmatrix}\partial u/\partial x&\partial u/\partial y\\\partial v/\partial x&\partial v/\partial y\end{vmatrix} \\ &=\begin{vmatrix}1&1\\1&4\end{vmatrix} \\ &=3.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}\right)^{-1}=\frac{1}{3}
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

Solving these affine equations also gives

$$
x=\frac{4 u}{3} - \frac{v}{3},\qquad y=- \frac{u}{3} + \frac{v}{3}.
$$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D 2 \left(x + y\right) e^{x + 4 y}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y&=\iint_\Delta 2 u e^{v}\,\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}v \\ &=\iint_\Delta 2 u e^{v}\,\left|\frac{1}{3}\right|\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}v \\ &=\frac{2}{3}\cdot \int_{0}^{3}\int_{1}^{4}u e^{v}\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}v \\ &=\frac{2}{3}\cdot \int_{0}^{3}e^{v}\,\mathrm{d}v\cdot \int_{1}^{4}u\,\mathrm{d}u \\ &=\frac{2}{3}\cdot \left[e^{v}\right]_{0}^{3}\cdot \left[\frac{u^{2}}{2}\right]_{1}^{4} \\ &=\frac{2}{3}\cdot \left(e^{3}-\left(e^{0}\right)\right)\cdot \left(\left(4\right)^{2}/2-\left(\left(1\right)^{2}/2\right)\right) \\ &=\frac{2}{3}\cdot \left(\left(e^{3}\right)-\left(1\right)\right)\cdot \left(\left(8\right)-\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\right) \\ &=\frac{2}{3}\cdot \left(-1 + e^{3}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{15}{2}\right) \\ &=-5 + 5 e^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the volume bounded by the region $R,$ given by

$$
R=\big\{(x,y,z)\, :\, 0\le 3 x\le 5,\quad 0\le 2 x + y\le 6,\quad 0\le 2 z\le 4\big\}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the volume of $R$ can be found as 

$$
V={∭}_{R}\text{d}V.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To compute the required volume, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

The inequalities that define the region $R,$

$$
0\le 3 x\le 5,\quad 0\le 2 x + y\le 6,\quad 0\le 2 z\le 4,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables

$$
u=3 x,\quad v=2 x + y,\quad w=2 z.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
T^{-1}:(x,y,z)\longmapsto(u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z)).
$$

To compute the required volume, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\Delta=\big\{(u,v,w):0\le u\le 5,\quad 0\le v\le 6,\quad 0\le w\le 4\big\}.
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial w}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left(3\right)(-1)^{1+1}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix}+\left(0\right)(-1)^{1+2}\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix}+\left(0\right)(-1)^{1+3}\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}\right)^{-1}=\frac{1}{6}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

The map to $R$ is

$$
T(u,v,w)=\left(\frac{u}{3},- \frac{2 u}{3} + v,\frac{w}{2}\right).
$$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iiint_R\mathrm{d}V & =\iiint_\Delta 1\cdot |\frac{1}{6}|\,\mathrm{d}u\mathrm{d}v\mathrm{d}w \\  & =\int_{0}^{5}\int_{0}^{6}\int_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{6}\,\mathrm{d}w\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot \int_{0}^{5}1\,\mathrm{d}u\cdot \int_{0}^{6}1\,\mathrm{d}v\cdot \int_{0}^{4}1\,\mathrm{d}w \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot [u]_{0}^{5}\cdot [v]_{0}^{6}\cdot [w]_{0}^{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot \left(\left(\left(5\right)\right)-\left(\left(0\right)\right)\right)\cdot \left(\left(\left(6\right)\right)-\left(\left(0\right)\right)\right)\cdot \left(\left(\left(4\right)\right)-\left(\left(0\right)\right)\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot \left(\left(5\right)-\left(0\right)\right)\cdot \left(\left(6\right)-\left(0\right)\right)\cdot \left(\left(4\right)-\left(0\right)\right) \\  & =20\end{aligned}
$$
